config.title: Forms & Validation (TypeScript)

intro.title: Forms & Validation — Typed
intro.body: You’ll build a small sign-up flow: typed state, controlled inputs, and validation the user sees right away—not after submit.
intro.usecase: Sign-up and profile forms are everywhere; getting state, events, and validation right here carries directly into production apps.

objectives: Model form data with a TypeScript interface and object state
Wire controlled inputs (value + onChange) to that state
Show inline validation errors as the user types

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: At the top of the file, import React and the useState hook from the `react` package.
steps.hint: Use a single import: default `React` plus the named hook `useState` from `'react'`.
steps.whyThisMatters: React comes with built-in tools called hooks that help you manage things like state, side effects, and shared logic.Your job isn't to build state management from scratch — it's to know which hook to reach for and bring it in. Imports are how you claim that work.

thinkPrompt.question: You're building a form component that needs to remember what the user is typing. React has a hook for exactly this. Which one do you reach for?
options: useEffect — runs side effects after render
useRef — grabs a direct reference to a DOM element
useState — holds and updates a value between renders
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: useState — holds and updates a value between renders

steps.anchor: For values that change as the user types, `useState` is the hook: it stores state and triggers re-renders when you update it—exactly what controlled inputs need.
steps.expectedOutcome: A valid import line that brings in `React` and `useState`.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—`React` and `useState` are in place. Next you’ll define the `FormState` interface for your fields.
steps.feedbackPartial: You still need both: default `React` and named `useState` from `'react'`.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: `import React, { useState } from 'react'` (or equivalent with both names from `'react'`).

steps.title: Define form state interface
steps.instruction: Below your imports, define a `FormState` interface at **module scope** with `name`, `email`, and `password`, each typed as `string`. Declare it outside any component—not inside a function body.
steps.hint: Use `interface FormState { … }` below the import line; field names should match the input `name` attributes you’ll use later. You’ll add `SignUpForm` in the next step.
steps.analogousExample: interface User { id: number; username: string; };
steps.whyThisMatters: In TypeScript, an interface describes the shape of your data — what fields exist and what type each field is. Think of it as a contract: anything that uses this data must follow the same rules. Instead of describing the shape every time you use it, you define it once and reference it by name everywhere.

thinkPrompt.question: Why define an interface for form state instead of using inline types?
options: Interfaces make the code run faster
Interfaces provide reusable, self-documenting type definitions
Multiple parts of your component — state, handlers, props — need to agree on the same shape. A named interface is the single source of truth; inline types force you to repeat or drift.
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Multiple parts of your component — state, handlers, props — need to agree on the same shape. A named interface is the single source of truth; inline types force you to repeat or drift.

steps.anchor: One named interface is the shared contract: state, handlers, and future props can all reference FormState instead of repeating or drifting inline shapes. At module scope it is defined once, easy to export, and matches typical TypeScript project layout.
steps.simplerVersion: type FormData = { field1: string; field2: string; };
steps.expectedOutcome: A module-level `FormState` interface with your three string fields.
successCriteria: Interface is defined at module scope (below imports), not inside a component body
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—`FormState` is at module scope and names the three fields you’ll bind to inputs and state.
steps.feedbackPartial: Declare `interface FormState` with `name`, `email`, and `password` as `string`—at file level, not inside a component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add `interface FormState { name: string; email: string; password: string; }` below your imports (not inside a component).

steps.title: Define the component
steps.instruction: Define a component named `SignUpForm` that renders JSX and declares an explicit return type of `JSX.Element`. Place it **below** your `FormState` interface.
steps.hint: Either an arrow component `const SignUpForm = (): JSX.Element => …` or `function SignUpForm(): JSX.Element { … }` works.
steps.whyThisMatters: The component is the shell: everything else (state, handlers, inputs) will live inside it.

thinkPrompt.question: What TypeScript type should a functional component return?

steps.anchor: `JSX.Element` is what you actually return from `<form>…</form>`—so the signature matches the UI.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed `SignUpForm` component you can add hooks and JSX inside.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice—`SignUpForm` is declared with a clear `JSX.Element` return. You can add state and markup next.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the name `SignUpForm` and an explicit `: JSX.Element` (or equivalent) on the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Declare `SignUpForm` so it returns JSX and type the return as `JSX.Element`.

steps.title: Initialize form state
steps.instruction: Create state with `useState<FormState>` and initialize `{ name: '', email: '', password: '' }`.
steps.hint: Destructure as `[formState, setFormState]`—the initial object must satisfy `FormState`.
steps.whyThisMatters: Typed `useState` means every update must produce a full `FormState` object (or you spread from `prev`).

thinkPrompt.question: What should the initial form state typically be?
options: Empty strings or default values matching the interface
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Empty strings or default values matching the interface

steps.anchor: Empty strings (or other defaults) should still satisfy `FormState`—no missing keys.
successCriteria: State is typed with the interface
Initial value has all three fields as empty strings
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—starting from empty strings matches typical sign-up defaults and pairs with controlled inputs.
steps.feedbackPartial: Use `useState<FormState>` and an initial object with `name`, `email`, and `password` set to `''`.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: `const [formState, setFormState] = useState<FormState>({ name: '', email: '', password: '' });`.

steps.title: Create the form JSX structure
steps.instruction: Return a `<form>` with three inputs: name (text), email (`type="email"`), and password (`type="password"`). Give each input a `name` that matches your state keys.
steps.hint: Semantic types (`email`, `password`) help browsers and accessibility; `name` will pair with your handler.
steps.whyThisMatters: You’re laying out the fields you’ll control with `value` / `onChange` in the next steps.

thinkPrompt.question: Which HTML element should wrap related form inputs?

steps.anchor: `<form>` groups related controls; native behavior (e.g. Enter to submit) and assistive tech expect it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A `<form>` containing three labeled inputs ready to wire to state.
successCriteria: Inputs have appropriate types (text, email, password)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—three inputs with sensible `type`s and `name`s set you up for one shared change handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: Wrap fields in `<form>` and include three `<input>` elements with `text`, `email`, and `password` as appropriate.
steps.feedbackWrong: Return `<form>…</form>` with three inputs; use `name="name"`, `name="email"`, `name="password"` (or consistent names matching state).

steps.title: Create change handler
steps.instruction: Add a `handleChange` that takes `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` and updates `formState` using `e.target.name` and `e.target.value` (spread the previous state so other fields stay intact).
steps.hint: `setFormState(prev => ({ ...prev, [e.target.name]: e.target.value }))` keeps one handler for all named inputs.
steps.whyThisMatters: One typed handler can serve every field as long as `name` matches a key on `FormState`.

thinkPrompt.question: What TypeScript type should we use for input change events?

steps.anchor: `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` narrows `target` to an input so `value` and `name` are available with correct types.
steps.simplerVersion: setFormState(prev => ({ ...prev, name: e.target.value })) // one field only
steps.expectedOutcome: A `handleChange` that updates the matching `FormState` key without dropping the others.
successCriteria: Updates form state using e.target.name and e.target.value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—typed event + dynamic key update is the usual pattern for multi-field forms.
steps.feedbackPartial: Ensure the parameter type is `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` and state updates use both `e.target.name` and `e.target.value`.
steps.feedbackWrong: Define `handleChange` with `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` and merge `e.target.value` into state under `[e.target.name]`.

steps.title: Connect inputs to state and handler
steps.instruction: Make each input controlled: set `value` from `formState` and `onChange={handleChange}`. Keep `name` aligned with your state keys (`name`, `email`, `password`).
steps.hint: Pattern per field: `value={formState.email}` and `name="email"` (and likewise for the others).
steps.whyThisMatters: Controlled inputs let validation and UI stay in sync because every keystroke flows through React state.

thinkPrompt.question: What two attributes create a controlled input in React?

steps.anchor: `value` shows what’s in state; `onChange` writes user input back—together they keep a single source of truth.
steps.expectedOutcome: Three controlled inputs reading from and writing to `formState`.
successCriteria: Inputs have value attributes bound to form state
Inputs have onChange attributes bound to handleChange
Each input has a name attribute matching its field
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice—state drives what’s on screen, and typing flows back through `handleChange`.
steps.feedbackPartial: Each input needs `value={…}`, `onChange={handleChange}`, and a `name` that matches a `FormState` key.
steps.feedbackWrong: Bind `value` to `formState.<field>`, pass `onChange={handleChange}`, and set `name` to the same key string.

steps.title: Add real-time validation
steps.instruction: Show inline errors as the user types: if email doesn’t include `'@'`, or password has fewer than 6 characters, render a short message (e.g. under that field).
steps.hint:
Derive booleans from `formState.email` / `formState.password` and use `&&` or a ternary to show `

` (or similar) only when invalid.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because inputs are controlled, you can recompute validity on every render from current state.

thinkPrompt.question: When should validation typically run in a form?

steps.anchor: Validating while typing surfaces problems before submit—users fix issues in context.
steps.expectedOutcome: Visible, inline feedback for email format and password length.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good—you’re reflecting rules in the UI as state changes, which is how most product forms behave.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check both rules: email must include `@`; password `length` must be at least 6. Show messages when they fail.
steps.feedbackWrong: Conditionally render errors when `!formState.email.includes('@')` or `formState.password.length < 6` (or equivalent).
